title: Toll Fermentation in Dead Alt-Protein Plants
one_liner: Buy or lease bankrupt alt-protein bioreactor capacity for pennies and run it as a toll fermenter for whey-alternative brands.
customer: Precision-fermentation whey and casein brands at Series A/B stage, plus protein buyers who need non-dairy supply.
problem: More than 70 alt-protein companies have merged or shut since Sept 2024, leaving idle fermentation assets, while whey is sold out and brands like Verley have product and FDA clearance but not plant capacity.
solution: Acquire or option distressed fermenters and downstream-processing lines, retool them into a multi-tenant toll plant, and sign take-or-pay reservations with whey-alternative brands.
why_now: H1 2026 alt-protein funding was only $197M (of which $132M fermentation), assets are cheap, and whey concentrate is up 108% in two years with buyers shifting from ESG goals to supply-risk mitigation.
revenue_model: Toll fee per kg processed plus take-or-pay capacity reservation fees; asset purchase is financed by anchor-tenant contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The sector's collapse is a capacity bargain arriving exactly when demand for non-dairy protein flipped from a values purchase to a supply-security purchase. The assets are worth more to a toll operator than to their bankrupt owners.
first_30_days: Catalogue stranded plants through bankruptcy brokers and lender sale lists, get LOIs from 2-3 whey-alternative brands for reserved capacity, and take a purchase or lease option on one plant contingent on an anchor contract.

title: Sway Sensors for Liability Trees
one_liner: Clamp-on accelerometer nodes that learn each high-consequence tree's own sway signature and alert arborists when it changes, turning one-off tree risk assessments into a recurring monitored service.
customer: Owners of trees with large liability tails: campgrounds and RV parks, historic estates and cemeteries, school districts, HOAs, golf courses and city parks departments. Channel: consulting arborists with tree-risk qualifications, and public-entity insurers and risk pools.
problem: Tree risk assessment is a visual snapshot repeated every few years, yet storms and root decay can change risk overnight. Falling trees kill people in campgrounds and parks and generate large claims. Owners can't watch hundreds of trees, and arborists have no recurring revenue stream.
solution: A MEMS accelerometer and inclinometer node on the trunk (BOM in the tens of dollars) reporting sway frequency, damping and static tilt over LoRaWAN. Each tree is modeled against its own baseline plus local wind data. Anomalies such as a drop in natural frequency or new tilt trigger an arborist inspection within 24 hours. Annual reports combine the data with the arborist's assessment as a documented notice-and-response record. Deploy on the top 5-10% of trees over targets: tent pads, cabins, playgrounds.
why_now: Published work now supports the approach: LoRaWAN tree-tilt systems recorded failure modes during a super typhoon, and 2025-26 papers validate low-cost MEMS inclinometers and accelerometers for tree stability analysis. Cheap LoRaWAN gateways and stronger storm and drought volatility raise demand.
revenue_model: USD 8-15 per sensor per month plus a USD 99 hardware deposit. Arborist resellers keep about 30% and bill their own assessments. A 40-tree campground is about USD 6k per year. Insurer-funded programs for risk pools later.
non_obvious_insight: Don't try to predict failure. Trees differ, so each tree's own baseline is the model and change is the signal. The buyer's real purchase is documented reasonable care: proof of what they knew and when they acted. That also flips arborists from selling a triennial visual inspection to owning a recurring alert service.
first_30_days: Put off-the-shelf LoRa accelerometer nodes on 20 trees with two consulting arborists and one friendly campground or state park. Collect 90 days of sway data across a wind season. Partner with a university forestry program for validation and a publishable result. Sell the first pilot subscriptions to campgrounds at about USD 600 per year per site.

title: Plumber Doorstep Network for Lead Line Access
one_liner: Sell water utilities and their engineering consultants a local-plumber network that verifies unknown service-line materials, converts homeowner access agreements and does the interior tie-ins on lead and galvanized line replacements.
customer: Municipal and regional water utilities (10k-200k connections) with a large 'unknown material' share in their lead service line inventory, and the engineering consultants running their inventories and replacement programs, funded by state revolving funds and Bipartisan Infrastructure Law money.
problem: Utilities must identify every unknown-material service line and replace lead and galvanized-requiring-replacement lines, including the private side, under the federal Lead and Copper Rule Improvements; several states (Michigan, New Jersey, Illinois) have their own mandates. The bottleneck is not excavation, it is access. Mailer response rates are low, homeowner self-identification is unreliable, and people do not want a stranger from Public Works in the basement. The utility's excavation contractor also usually refuses to touch interior plumbing, so the interior reconnection sits in limbo. EPA's own August 2026 access-tips document exists because this is where programs stall.
solution: A branded 'Local Plumber Verification' visit. A licensed plumber or apprentice from a local shop knocks on a scheduled visit, checks the pipe where it enters the house (scratch and magnet test, the wiped-joint bulge, meter connection, photo protocol) in about 10 minutes, and uploads a GIS-ready record to the inventory. They get the access agreement signed on the spot, note obstructions (finished basement, boxed-in pipe, shutoff condition) and pre-scope the interior tie-in. A second product is the interior tie-in and shutoff replacement, done by the same shops as a subcontract to the utility's excavation contractor, with a warranty on the house side.
why_now: The federal rule's ten-year replacement clock, the compliance dates approaching in 2027, EPA's freshly updated access guidance, and billions in SRF and BIL money that has to be spent all converge. Utilities are now measured on unknown-line reduction, and consultants are looking for boots on the ground. Even if federal deadlines are softened, the state laws and the fact that unknown lines still have to be identified keep the demand.
revenue_model: $60-120 per verified line, $150-300 per signed access agreement (both paid by utility or consultant per unit), and a 15-20% margin on interior tie-in subcontracts ($400-1,500 each). The shop keeps most of the field labor and pays the network for lead flow, tooling, quality control and the reporting workflow.
non_obvious_insight: Homeowners trust the truck with a local plumber's name on it far more than a city letter, and the plumber can read a lead line faster than any model can read a mailer. The reason programs stall is that homeowners fear that letting anyone in means they will be found to have a problem and get a bill, and that the utility contractor will leave their basement half-connected. A plumber solves both, and plumbers are the only people who already have a license, insurance and an interior-work warranty.
first_30_days: Skip direct municipal procurement at first and sell to a mid-size engineering consultant who already holds the utility's inventory contract and needs subcontractors. Pick two utilities with a high unknown share and low mailer response. Propose a paid pilot of 300 addresses at a fixed price per verification. Recruit 3 shops that want steady work for apprentices. Build the mobile form and photo protocol in a form tool that exports to the utility's inventory template.

title: Scam-Spell Breakers: Human Callbacks for Seniors
one_liner: A human 'callback' service in which ex-call-center agents are trained to talk older customers out of scams, sold to credit unions and community banks as a per-member protection benefit.
customer: Community banks and credit unions (5k-200k members), also Medicare Advantage plans, and families via a $19/month consumer plan. Banks pay about $0.40-1.00 per member per month or $75-150 per intervention.
problem: The FBI's 2025 IC3 report (April 2026) shows Americans over 60 lost $7.75B, up 59%, with more than 3,100 senior complaints citing AI. Detection systems flag transactions, but victims coached by scammers ignore warnings and lie to tellers. Frontline staff lack the time and training for the delicate conversation that breaks the scammer's hold without shaming the victim.
solution: When a bank's system flags a large or unusual transfer by a senior, the transaction is held and a trained spell-breaker calls within minutes. They use scam-specific playbooks (romance, crypto investment, tech support) based on motivational interviewing, guide the customer to verify independently with a trusted family member, and document the outcome. They also enroll a trusted-contact circle and run monthly check-ins. Reports show dollars saved per dollar of fees.
why_now: Elder-fraud losses and AI-voice-clone scams are rising sharply, while banks face regulatory and reputational pressure to show duty of care. Call-center layoffs create a large pool of people with exactly this skill set.
revenue_model: Per-member-per-month bank contracts, per-intervention fees, a consumer family plan, and outcome-based bonuses tied to verified saves.
non_obvious_insight: Scam interception is a rapport problem, not a detection problem, and the best call-center agents' skills of de-escalation, listening, and warm scripts transfer directly. The ROI is unusually crisp for a services business: dollars saved versus fees, which gives an easy pitch to a CFO or board.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 ex-agents and train them with retired fraud investigators and a social worker. Approach 3 credit unions through state leagues and offer a 90-day, success-priced pilot using the credit union's existing fraud alerts and a purely phone-based workflow. Aim for one paid pilot within 60-90 days.

title: Heirloom Fair-Division Engine for Sibling Estates
one_liner: Use a fair-division algorithm and a phone walkthrough to split a dead parent's belongings so nobody feels cheated.
customer: Executors (often the eldest child), estate attorneys, mediators and professional fiduciaries. Families pay $149-$399 per estate, or attorneys pay $99/month.
problem: Research on inheritance conflict (for example the University of Minnesota's 'Who Gets Grandma's Yellow Pie Plate?' work) finds sentimental personal property, not money, triggers most sibling fights. Executors improvise with turn-taking or a spreadsheet, distant siblings get shortchanged, and the house can't be sold until it is cleared.
solution: A phone walkthrough captures the house room by room, AI tags items, and each remote heir gets a private points budget to express wants. A fair-division algorithm (adjusted-winner or envy-free-up-to-one-item style) proposes an allocation with cash or point equalization. The app then coordinates shipping and pickup, and routes leftovers to donation with receipts or to sale. It ends with a signed distribution memo the attorney can file. Each item keeps a story card so its history survives.
why_now: Multimodal AI can inventory objects from video, and phone-based 3D capture is mainstream. Boomer households hold decades of belongings that Millennial and Gen X heirs scattered across the country often don't want. With the federal estate tax largely out of the picture for most families (reported $15M exemption), family conflict is the main remaining risk.
revenue_model: Per-estate fee ($149-$399), 10-15% margin on shipping and donation logistics, and attorney seats at $99/month.
non_obvious_insight: The fights are about objects, not dollars. Objects are one of the few asset classes with a known mechanism-design solution, and no estate product uses it.
first_30_days: Build a no-code prototype with a spreadsheet points auction. Offer it free to 20 executors found in estate-help forums and groups. Ask elder-law attorneys to use it as a mediation-lite deliverable and convert 5 of them to paid. Time-box the whole thing to about three weeks per estate.

title: Crash-Test Ratings for Collusive Pricing Agents
one_liner: A simulation lab and clean-room negotiation venue that certifies your pricing or negotiating agent does not tacitly collude with counterpart agents, like Euro NCAP for antitrust.
customer: General counsel, antitrust counsel and pricing or procurement heads at companies deploying pricing or negotiation agents: property managers and landlords, hotels, insurers, freight brokers, ad-buying agencies and retailers. Pricing-software vendors who are being sued are the first buyers.
problem: Two LLM agents that repeatedly interact can converge on supracompetitive prices with no human ever agreeing to anything. The law is moving fast: California's AB 325 took effect January 1, 2026, the DOJ RealPage settlement landed in late 2025, and DOJ officials said in May 2026 that 'software cannot launder collusion'. Deployers have no way to show their agent is clean.
solution: A harness that plays your agent against a zoo of counterpart agents (clones of itself, competitor-like agents, vendor agents) across thousands of repeated-game scenarios. It measures price convergence, punishment and signaling patterns, and information leakage, and issues a rated report plus CI regression tests. A hosted clean-room negotiation venue firewalls competitors' inputs and keeps regulator-readable logs. Partner economists and an antitrust firm sign the report.
why_now: AB 325 and its lowered pleading standard, active DOJ and state enforcement, private class actions over pricing algorithms, and agent-to-agent negotiation going live with the 2026 commerce protocols. Academic work has shown LLM pricing agents can settle on collusive outcomes without instruction.
revenue_model: $25-150k per audit, $2-5k per month for CI-integrated monitoring, and expert-witness and defense-support add-ons revenue-shared with partner economists.
non_obvious_insight: The exculpatory evidence is counterfactual behavior: what your agent would do if a rival raised its price. Only the deployer can generate that evidence, and it is cheap to produce in simulation, so antitrust compliance can be turned into unit tests. Because plausible-agreement pleading is now enough to survive dismissal, having a dated, third-party test record is worth far more than its price.
first_30_days: Team up an industrial-organization economist and an antitrust lawyer. Publish an open 'collusion eval' benchmark of LLM repeated pricing games to build credibility. Pitch 10 rental-pricing, hospitality and freight-pricing software vendors a $25k fixed-fee 'pre-litigation' audit and close the first two within about 60 days.

title: Reliance Ratings for SOC 2 Reports and Auditors
one_liner: A buyer-paid forensic desk that tells vendor-risk teams how far to trust a given SOC 2 or ISO report, and the audit firm that signed it.
customer: Third-party-risk and security teams at banks, health systems, insurers and mid-market SaaS companies that ingest hundreds of vendor reports a year. Cyber insurers and PE/VC diligence teams are the second wave.
problem: In March 2026 a whistleblower alleged that Delve, a YC-backed startup valued at about $300M, issued 494 near-identical SOC 2 reports with conclusions pre-filled and signed by two rubber-stamp firms. YC removed it in April, and Delve disputes the claims. Buyers now suspect every clean PDF. Manual checks of AICPA peer-review and NASBA licence records take about 30 minutes per report, so most teams skip them.
solution: The buyer uploads the vendor's report. We compare it with a growing corpus using fuzzy fingerprints of system descriptions, test procedures and exception language. We check CPA licence, AICPA peer-review status, firm ownership, address and staffing footprint, sample sizes, period length, carve-outs and subservice-organisation scope. Output is a reliance score, a one-page red-flag memo, and a continuously updated rating of audit firms based on exception rates, boilerplate share and peer-review opinions.
why_now: The Delve fallout in spring 2026 made every security team ask 'who signed this?'. Compliance-automation platforms now tie vendors to audit-firm networks at scale (Vanta reports about 16,000 customers). LLMs make reading and comparing thousands of 80-page reports cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: $200-400 per report on demand, $20-60k per year TPRM subscriptions, API licences to vendor-risk platforms, and insurer portfolio scans.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat the audit as a commodity input that automation has solved. Audit quality varies enormously and invisibly, and the vendor pays its own auditor. That is the same conflict that made bond-rating agencies necessary. The moat is the corpus of reports, which only buyers collectively hold.
first_30_days: Build the fingerprint tool on 200 public reports from trust centres. Publish an 'Auditor Firm Quality Index v0' from public peer-review data. Offer security leads free re-verification of their vendor stack in exchange for contributing reports to the corpus, starting with those exposed to Delve's customer list.

title: Professional Health-Care Agents for Solo Agers
one_liner: A subscription 'designated agent' nurse-advocate with health-care proxy authority who is reachable at 2 am, sold to solo agers and to hospitals stuck with unbefriended patients.
customer: Solo agers 70-85 with $300k-$2M in assets and no spouse or children nearby (27% of 65+ live alone). Hospitals and elder-law attorneys are the B2B channels.
problem: Solo agers often lack a health-care proxy. When a crisis hits, hospitals face consent and discharge bottlenecks, and the state may appoint a professional guardian through a slow, expensive court process. Agencies and hospitals can't act as trusted agents because of conflicts of interest.
solution: A nurse- or social-worker-led firm whose individual employees serve as named health-care agents. It handles values interviews and updated directives, a wallet card and QR code hospitals can scan to reach the on-call agent, monthly check-ins, and in-hospital advocacy during admissions and discharge. It coordinates with a separate financial fiduciary. AI documentation tools let one agent serve 60-80 clients. Hospitals can also contract for surrogate support for unbefriended patients.
why_now: Solo-ager demographics and the 80+ cohort are surging (NPR, Jul 2026). SNF and home-care capacity is tightening, so discharge delays cost hospitals more, and family caregivers are stretched by Medicaid retrenchment.
revenue_model: $2,400-4,800 a year subscription plus hourly rates for hospital stays, and $1,500-3,000 per unbefriended-patient episode from hospitals.
non_obvious_insight: Care is available if you can pay, but a trusted person with legal authority who answers at 2 am is the missing product. Because family-based caregiving is the default assumption, almost every caregiver product targets a family that doesn't exist for this cohort.
first_30_days: In one state with friendly proxy law (Washington, Oregon or Colorado), recruit two RN or MSW advocates, sign 10 clients through estate attorneys, and approach two hospital case-management directors with a pilot for unbefriended patients.

title: Immigration Deadline Sentinel for Work-Permit Households
one_liner: The wealthy keep immigration counsel on retainer to calendar, file early and bridge gaps; for $20/mo, give H-4, OPT, asylum-applicant and DACA households an encrypted deadline vault and family-readiness plan.
customer: Households whose work authorization depends on renewable USCIS documents: H-4/L-2 spouses with EADs, F-1 OPT/STEM OPT students, asylum applicants, DACA recipients, and pending adjustment applicants. Sold at $20/mo per household, or $4-8 per head through employers, university international offices, credit unions and churches.
problem: DHS ended automatic 540-day EAD extensions for renewals filed on or after 30 October 2025. USCIS advises filing up to 180 days early, yet some I-765 categories are reported at many months to a year or more, so gaps in work authorization mean lost jobs, licenses and health coverage. Rich families' lawyers prevent this by tracking every date; ordinary families rely on memory and WhatsApp.
solution: An end-to-end-encrypted vault, on-device where possible: photograph an EAD, I-94 or I-797 and it extracts dates and builds a household calendar (EAD file window opening at day 180, AR-11 address change within 10 days, OPT unemployment day counter, I-751, N-400 windows, passport expiries). It pre-fills renewal packets for attorney review, generates employer bridging letters, and monitors case status. For cases outside normal processing times it prepares a congressional-inquiry package. It adds a family-readiness plan (power of attorney, standby guardianship for children, contact tree, know-your-rights card). Flat-fee referrals go to attorneys and DOJ-accredited representatives. It is software and documents, not legal advice.
why_now: The October 2025 interim final rule ended automatic extensions, processing times are long, USCIS moved to a new I-765 form version (mandatory from March 2026), and enforcement anxiety is high in 2026. Employers and universities are scrambling to protect workers.
revenue_model: $20/mo per household; $3-6 per employee per month for employer or university dashboards; flat referral fees from partner attorneys; enterprise HR reporting tier.
non_obvious_insight: Wealthy people's immigration counsel adds most of its value before a crisis, by calendaring, filing early and pre-drafting backups, which software can supply for a fraction of the cost. Privacy-by-design (end-to-end encryption so a subpoena or breach yields nothing) is not just compliance but the differentiator for a population that fears data exposure. The paying wedge is the professional H-4/OPT segment and their employers, not the most vulnerable households.
first_30_days: Build a WhatsApp and spreadsheet MVP that ingests document photos and sends reminders. Partner with 2 immigration attorneys on flat-fee referral, 3 university international offices, and H-4 spouse and OPT Facebook groups. Enroll 100 households free, convert to $20/mo, and pilot with one employer HR team.

title: Vetted Remote Operators for Home Robots
one_liner: A privacy-audited, background-checked, insured pool of remote operators who take over home and warehouse robots at their hard moments, sold to robot makers as the trust layer for teleoperation.
customer: Home-robot, service-robot and warehouse-robot makers pay $18-35 per operator-hour. Operators are displaced support and ops workers earning $22-30 an hour.
problem: The first consumer humanoids (such as 1X's NEO) ship in 2026 relying on remote humans who can see inside homes, which raised a privacy backlash. Robot startups lack a scalable, vetted, insured operator workforce and would otherwise use anonymous offshore BPOs, while buyers want accountable domestic operators.
solution: Recruit and train from displaced call-centre, ops and gaming talent. A standard teleop certification, privacy protocols (blurred or avatarised feeds, no recording, no-go zones), session audit logs, background checks and E&O/cyber insurance form the service. Scheduling covers time zones and performance metrics track intervention success. Start with warehouse or delivery robots, then homes.
why_now: Consumer humanoid preorders and shipments began in 2025-26 with teleop as the fallback, warehouse and sidewalk robots are at scale, and privacy concerns make trust a differentiator.
revenue_model: 30-40% margin per operator-hour, certification fees and an insurance premium share.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for robots is not hardware but trusted remote labor, and every teleop intervention also trains the policy. Privacy trust, not price, is the moat, and it reframes displaced workers as a new 'robot pilot' class.
first_30_days: Contact 20 robotics startups (delivery, warehouse, cleaning) with a pilot of 5 vetted operators for 200 hours at cost. Write the privacy protocol and audit template. Recruit 30 candidates from laid-off support and ops staff.

title: Contingency Refunds for Fake Local-Service Leads
one_liner: A win-based service that audits what plumbers, HVAC firms, locksmiths, law offices and clinics pay per lead or call, proves which were bots, spam or out-of-area, and files the platform disputes owners never get around to.
customer: Owner-operators of 1-20 person home-service, legal and clinic businesses spending $1.5K-15K/month on Google Local Services Ads, Thumbtack, Angi, Yelp and tracked call numbers. Fee is 25% of credits recovered.
problem: 'Reaching customers' is the number-one small-business challenge (Fed SBCS 2026) while legacy local-marketing vendors shrink (Thryv 2025 revenue $785M, down). Owners pay per lead but cannot tell real jobs from junk, and platform dispute windows are short and evidence-heavy, so credits likely go unclaimed (my inference; recovery rates need testing). Bot share of web traffic is estimated anywhere from about 20% (Cloudflare CEO) to over 50% (Imperva/Fortune), and cheap AI voice agents make robo-calls to paid numbers easier.
solution: The owner connects ad and lead accounts or forwards lead emails and call-tracking numbers. The system transcribes calls, scores caller numbers, checks geography and duplicates, classifies wrong-service and spam leads, and flags synthetic voices. It assembles evidence and files disputes inside each platform's window, reconciles the credits, and reports a monthly verified-lead rate per channel to guide budget.
why_now: Speech-to-text and classification now cost pennies per call. AI-generated traffic is polluting pay-per-lead channels while platform-native verification stays thin. Small owners have less time and money than ever, and outcome-priced recovery is exactly what subscription incumbents cannot easily offer.
revenue_model: 25% of credits recovered, plus a $49/month scorecard after month 3. Later add white-label to marketing agencies and sell verified-lead-rate benchmarks.
non_obvious_insight: Platforms already built refund mechanisms and profit from friction, so packaging evidence on time is the whole product. The independent verified-lead rate per channel is the first honest ROI data most SMBs ever get, and it may end up worth more than the refunds. Contingency pricing works because credits appear as visible cash in the ad account.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 owners from HVAC, garage-door, locksmith and plumber Facebook groups with a free 60-day lookback audit. Contract VAs to file disputes manually and measure recovery as a percent of spend. Publish a junk-lead-rate benchmark by platform, and build software only once recovery exceeds roughly 8% of spend.

title: Sewage Nielsen: Wastewater Consumption Index
one_liner: Weekly per-capita consumption of alcohol, nicotine, cannabis and caffeine, measured from metabolites in city wastewater and sold to alt-data funds and regulators as a Nielsen for vices.
customer: Alt-data-buying hedge funds and long-only consumer analysts covering alcohol, tobacco and nicotine pouches, cannabis and energy drinks. Secondary: state cannabis and tax regulators who want to size legal versus illicit share, and cannabis operators or beverage companies buying custom market studies.
problem: Investors debating whether GLP-1 drugs and Gen Z are actually cutting alcohol, or whether nicotine pouches and cannabis are cannibalizing other products, rely on lagging, self-reported or scanner data. Those sources miss the illicit, gray-market, direct-to-consumer and cash segments. Regulators cannot measure the illicit cannabis share either.
solution: Composite-sample assays at 15-25 wastewater treatment plants across major metros, run weekly by a partner analytical lab (LC-MS/MS). Measure alcohol (ethyl sulfate), nicotine (cotinine), cannabis (THC-COOH) and caffeine metabolites. Normalize with population markers and flow to get per-capita consumption estimates. Only report at sewersheds serving 50k+ people, which handles privacy. Deliver as a weekly index via API and CSV with methodology notes. Sell a historical series built from archived samples.
why_now: The GLP-1 alcohol-reduction debate is a live equity question. Nicotine pouches and cannabis regulation are moving fast. Wastewater programs built with pandemic-era public health funding are shrinking or uncertain, which leaves utilities, university labs, sampling gear and freezer archives idle and open to co-funding. Alt-data budgets keep growing and funds want signals with no retail-panel bias.
revenue_model: Alt-data subscription of roughly 60-250k USD per year per fund, with tiered metro coverage. Government and regulator contracts (illicit-market sizing). Custom brand or category studies of 25-100k USD. Later, per-sewershed expansions paid by cities as a public-health co-benefit.
non_obvious_insight: Sewage is the only consumption panel that cannot be gamed, self-reported or missed by scanner data, because it captures what people actually consume regardless of channel. The science has been used by European drug-monitoring networks for 15 years, but nobody has packaged it as a consumer-sector economic indicator. Pandemic-era freezer archives of stored samples let you sell a multi-year backtestable history on day one, which is the thing quant buyers require before they will pay.
first_30_days: Partner with a university lab that already has validated LC-MS/MS methods for these metabolites and old COVID-monitoring relationships with treatment plants. Sign MOUs with 3-5 plants. Run assays on archived samples to build a 2021-2025 backtest series for those sewersheds. Pitch 15 alt-data funds and data-aggregator marketplaces with the backtest chart of one hook (for example alcohol per-capita against local retail sales). Launch a pilot at 5 sewersheds with 2-3 design-partner funds paying pilot fees. Note that the plan depends on plant access agreements and lab throughput.

title: White-Label Camera Forensics for Cities and Schools
one_liner: Scan municipal and school camera, recorder and IoT fleets to unmask white-labeled hardware with covered Hikvision or Dahua internals and produce grant-ready compliance attestations and phased replacement plans.
customer: City and county IT and police departments, school districts, transit agencies and the MSPs and integrators serving them. They pay $3-15k per fleet audit plus an annual monitoring fee.
problem: Federal grant terms (DOJ, DHS and FEMA, school-safety programs) bar covered surveillance equipment under NDAA Section 889 and 2 CFR 200.216, including where it is a substantial or essential component of a system sold under another brand. Many fleets bought 2015-2020 contain OEM boards nobody can trace, and the integrator who sold them has a conflict in saying so. Sensor stacking (noise detectors on license-plate readers) is spreading while surveillance-vendor scrutiny grows.
solution: An agentless scanner that fingerprints devices by firmware, banners, MAC ranges and cloud endpoints (including peer-to-peer relay services) to reveal OEM lineage across cameras, NVRs, access panels and doorbells. Output is an asset inventory, a grant-attestation letter, and a replacement plan sequenced against grant cycles, with domestic or trade-compliant alternatives. Integrators pay a referral fee for replacement work.
why_now: Compliance is now BOM-level across industries, and grant conditions are being enforced more tightly. Cities face ADA Title II (Apr 2027) and CJIS 6.0 (Oct 2027) deadlines that already force IT audits. Public backlash over camera vendors makes proof of diligence politically valuable.
revenue_model: $3-15k per fleet audit, $1-3 per device per year for monitoring and re-scan, and 3-8% referral fees on replacement projects. Sell through MSPs and state cooperative contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance is defined by the chip in the box, not the label on the box. Origin lineage of white-labeled OEM electronics is an unpriced supply-chain data problem that only shows up at the moment a city touches federal money, and the fingerprint database becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Release a free 'Is my camera a Hikvision?' desktop scanner for IT staff as lead-gen, audit 3 school districts at cost to build the fingerprint set, and then sell $5k audits to the first 5 districts via grant writers and state school-safety offices.

title: H.264 Royalty Sunset Desk for Streamers
one_liner: A country-by-country patent-expiry analysis and codec-delivery plan that cuts H.264/AVC streaming royalty exposure for mid-tier video services, paid partly on savings.
customer: Mid-size OTT and FAST channel operators, ed-tech, fitness, telehealth and cloud-gaming platforms and video-heavy social apps (well below the 100M-subscriber mega-tier). Buyer is the general counsel, CFO or head of video engineering.
problem: The Via LA AVC pool replaced its flat $100k streaming cap with tiered fees up to $4.5M a year, and added FAST and cloud-gaming categories, for a codec standardized in 2003. Press reports say US patent coverage runs out around 2028, so one analysis says paying $4.5M for about 18 months of coverage 'makes no economic sense'. Wikipedia and HN commenters put at least one US patent at 2030 and 'only 5 left' worldwide. Mid-tier operators can't tell what they actually owe.
solution: Ingest Via LA's public AVC patent attachment (re-issued 2026-09-28) plus national legal-status data, and build a live-patent map per country. Overlay each customer's audience by country and device. Deliver (a) a counsel-ready exposure memo to negotiate the right tier or challenge scope, (b) an engineering plan that serves AV1/VP9 in territories with live patents and H.264 where none remain, using a device-capability ladder, and (c) a countdown dashboard that also tracks HEVC and audio codecs. Work with a patent attorney partner so the memo is legal work product.
why_now: The new streaming fee schedule took effect in early 2026 (Tom's Hardware, Apr 3, 2026: fees raised 'from $100,000 up to $4.5 million'). The last MPEG-4 Part 2 patent expired 2026-07-19 and the last E-AC3 patents may have lapsed in 2026, so 'is it free yet?' is a live question. AV1 hardware decode is now common in 2023+ phones, TVs and PCs.
revenue_model: Fixed $15k-$40k audit and plan, plus about 20% of first-year royalty savings or avoided fees, plus $1k a month for the monitoring dashboard.
non_obvious_insight: Patent pools price by audience tier, not by how many patents are still alive, and patents are territorial and expire on different dates, so the expiry calendar itself is arbitrage. Evidence: Via LA's program page shows Tier 1 at $4.5M a year, small operators as low as $100k, new FAST and cloud-gaming tiers, and a patent attachment updated 2026-09-28 (https://www.via-la.com/licensing-2/avc-h-264/). The Wikipedia AVC entry notes many patents expired but at least one US patent runs to Nov 2030, and that Nokia sued HP and Amazon over H.264/H.265 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Video_Coding). The HN thread on the last Brazilian MPEG-4 patent expiring includes 'only 5 left' and a Siemens patent to 2030 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/49311814). Details of the expired Siemens BR patent: https://www.xda-developers.com/25-year-old-brazilian-video-patent-expired-legal-headache-linux/.
first_30_days: Days 1-14: scrape the Via LA patent list and build the per-country expiry table for AVC (a few weekends of work). Days 10-30: post the free 'H.264 patent death clock' as a public page, pitch 30 mid-size streaming and video-first SaaS companies from job boards and app-store data with a free exposure estimate, and offer a $7.5k pilot audit to the first 3 who reply. Retain a patent attorney on a flat fee to sign off on memo templates.

title: Licensed Principal-of-Record for Financial Agents
one_liner: Buy a retiring independent insurance agency, then rent its licenses, carrier appointments and supervision layer to AI-agent builders that need a legally accountable entity behind every quote and bind.
customer: Startups building consumer or SMB agents that quote, recommend or bind insurance (later, money-movement advice), plus independent agencies that want to deploy agents under compliance cover.
problem: An agent that solicits or binds coverage is doing a licensed activity, but software has no license. Fifty-state producer licensing and carrier appointments take years, so agent startups avoid the vertical, use lead-gen workarounds, or run unsupervised. Regulators are converging on the idea that a licensed entity must own what the AI says (the NAIC AI bulletin has been adopted by roughly two dozen states).
solution: Acquire one or two small independent agencies (about 1.5-2x revenue, seller-financed) and inherit their resident and non-resident licenses, appointments and renewal book. Onboard agent builders as sub-producers. Provide the supervision layer: conversation and decision logging, rule-based disclosure and suitability guardrails, escalation to a licensed human reviewer, E&O coverage and regulator-ready audit trails.
why_now: Independent agencies are shrinking (39k in 2024 to 37k in 2026), so owners are selling. About 95% of commercial insurance is still sold by humans. Q2 2026 insurtech funding hit $2.44B with 99.1% going to AI-centric firms (Outmarket raised $34.5M at a $335M valuation). ISO's generative-AI exclusion (CG 40 47) is pushing buyers to look for affirmative cover.
revenue_model: A 20-40% override on commissions from agent-originated policies, a monthly supervision and platform fee per agent-builder ($2-10k), and the acquired book's renewal commissions as base cash flow.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not the model but a clean license history plus carrier appointments, which a retiring agency owner will sell cheaply and whose renewal stream funds the company. Whoever becomes the accountable principal for autonomous sellers collects a toll on all of them, a US analog to the UK Appointed Representative regime.
first_30_days: Shortlist 5 agencies (owners 60+, $500k-$2M revenue, licensed in 10+ states) through perpetuation brokers and sign an LOI with seller financing on one. Sign 3 design partners (AI quoting or benefits-navigator startups) for shadow-mode onboarding. Get a written opinion from insurance-regulatory counsel on how AI-conducted solicitations are treated for sub-producers in the first 3 states.

title: Resin Swap Bureau for Shortage-Hit Molders
one_liner: Fast material-equivalency testing and paperwork for injection molders who must switch resin grades when supply breaks.
customer: Small and mid-size injection molders and extruders with 10-200 employees, and their OEM quality engineers (appliance, auto, medical, electrical).
problem: Hormuz transits run about 10 a day against a baseline of 88-130, and the Gulf is a large polymer and petrochemical exporter (my inference on resin exposure). ISM comments cite long lead times and price volatility. Molders forced to change resin need to requalify with UL recognition, food-contact letters, PPAP and customer sign-off, and testing labs take weeks.
solution: An equivalency database (datasheet parsing plus coupon results) and a fast-turn lab partner. For each part spec it ranks substitutes, runs a five-day test protocol (tensile, impact, heat deflection, melt flow, shrinkage, UL 94 screen, color), and produces the change package: process change notice, PPAP delta and customer approval draft. It tracks UL, FDA and REACH status.
why_now: The war shock and volatility force substitutions now, and lead times are stretching. Molders have no in-house materials engineers.
revenue_model: $2.5-8k per part-family qualification. About $6k a year for database and alerts. Margin on lab work.
non_obvious_insight: In a shortage, finding a substitute resin is easy because a distributor can suggest one. The bottleneck is proving to a customer's QA that the substitute is allowed. The valuable product is the paperwork.
first_30_days: Partner with a certified test lab. Sign five molders. Build the first 50 equivalency sets in one resin family (PP, ABS or PC) from public datasheets. Publish a free shortage swap guide to gather leads.

title: 48-Hour Patent Troll Response Desk for SMBs
one_liner: A flat-fee service that answers patent-troll demand letters within 48 hours with an AI-built claim chart, prior art, the assertion entity's litigation history and an attorney-signed response.
customer: Small e-commerce, restaurant-tech, app and SaaS companies (under about $20M revenue) receiving non-practicing-entity demand letters or complaints, plus IP insurers and trade associations that want a member benefit.
problem: Trolls price demands just below the cost of defense ($50k to $150k+), betting small targets will settle. Hourly-billing law firms can't respond cheaply, and the patent office's post-grant review path has gotten harder since 2025 with rising discretionary denials, though a March 2026 USPTO memo added small-business and domestic-manufacturing factors.
solution: 24-hour intake. LLM-assisted claim mapping of the patent to the target's product, a prior-art sweep, the patent's history (past invalidations, review petitions, family members, assignment chain), and the plaintiff's prior settlement pattern from court dockets. A partner patent attorney reviews and signs a response letter. Options: a shared 'campaign file' for other targets of the same troll, and an insured defense fund via membership.
why_now: Modern models can chart claims and search prior art in hours rather than billable weeks. Incumbent firms, paid by the hour, have little incentive to compress. The patent office's shifting policies make cheap district-court leverage more valuable.
revenue_model: Fixed $2.5k to $6k per response package, $99 to $299 monthly membership with pooled defense credits, and referral or insurance partnerships.
non_obvious_insight: The troll's model relies on low-cost, repeated assertion against many small targets, so it is undermined by a cheap, credible response and by a memory of it. Every response feeds a campaign file, and the second, third and hundredth target of the same entity get better and cheaper defense. That flips the network effect from the troll to the defenders, and word spreads fast that a target is not a soft settle.
first_30_days: Partner with one patent litigator on a flat-fee arrangement. Pull the top 20 active NPE campaigns from court dockets and pre-build claim-chart templates. Announce free 24-hour triage in small-business, Shopify and app-developer communities. Charge $3k for the first five full response packages.

title: Universal Insurance Claims Rails for Vet Front Desks
one_liner: Vet front desks lose hours filing claims in a dozen insurer portals; sell them one submission and status layer, then add pre-approval and instant-pay as insurers plug in.
customer: Independent clinics and small groups (1-20 locations) with 15-30% insured patients. Later, insurers as per-claim payers.
problem: There are about 6.98M insured animals (+9% in 2025), each insurer has its own portal, forms and record requests, and only 48.2% of practices proactively recommend insurance. Owners often front the full bill. Insurers cannot see clinics, so they lack pre-authorization, real-time pricing and fraud tools.
solution: A browser agent inside the PIMS invoice screen, later API-connected, sends invoice plus records to the right insurer by policy number, tracks status, chases missing documents and reconciles payments. Once volume gives risk data, offer a direct-pay advance so the owner only pays the deductible at checkout.
why_now: Insured animals keep growing while premiums outpace enrollment, so insurers want lower cost-to-adjudicate. Computer-use LLM agents can operate portals without waiting for API deals. Ambient scribes are producing more structured records for claims.
revenue_model: $99-199 per clinic per month, $1-3 per clean claim from insurers later, and a 2-3% fee on advanced claims.
non_obvious_insight: Insurance penetration is partly a back-office problem: the clinic is the distribution channel and is punished with admin work for recommending coverage. Remove the penalty and the recommendation rate rises. The clearinghouse owns the claims data insurers currently cannot see.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 clinics through cloud-PIMS user groups. Shadow the front desk for a week and automate the top 5 insurers by portal. Offer 30 days free, then $99 per month. Measure hours saved per week and days-to-payment.

title: Design-for-Duty: Engineer Below the 15% Metal Line
one_liner: A CAD/BOM tool that redesigns imported products to fall under Section 232's metal-weight cliffs or qualify for the 10% US-melt rate.
customer: Product-engineering and sourcing leads at $20M-$500M brands that import metal-heavy goods (furniture, fitness gear, grills, hand tools, lighting, enclosures, HVAC accessories).
problem: Since 2026-04-06 metals duties apply to full customs value: 50% on primary metal, 25% on derivatives, and 10% if made with US-melted steel or US-smelted aluminum/copper. Products under 15% metal weight are excluded (per Foley; verify current text). More derivative articles were proposed on 2026-08-06. Insiders treat this as a sourcing or lobbying problem. Brokers and freight forwarders cannot change a bill of materials, and engineers do not know the cliff exists.
solution: A plugin and standalone tool that ingests CAD mass properties and the BOM (SolidWorks, Fusion, Onshape or CSV). It computes metal weight share per SKU and simulates variants, such as a polymer or wood part in place of a steel bracket, or one US-melted component. It returns duty-weighted landed cost per variant and drafts the engineering change order. It also flags SKUs sitting just above a tier boundary.
why_now: The IEEPA tariffs fell on 2026-02-20 and the regime moved onto Section 232. Metal content is now the biggest variable in landed cost. Full-value duties began in April 2026, and the August 2026 proposal adds derivative products.
revenue_model: SaaS at $1.5-4k a month per product line. Launch-phase audits at $1.5k per SKU. Optional 10-15% share of first-year duty saved on redesigned SKUs.
non_obvious_insight: The tariff is a bill-of-materials problem, not a country problem. A few points of mass shifted can be worth more than moving a factory, and no one in the chain (broker, freight forwarder, sourcing agent) is paid to touch the design.
first_30_days: Pull public bill-of-lading data for HTS chapters exposed to metal derivatives. Cold-email 100 product heads offering a free one-SKU cliff check. Sell 10 fixed-price SKU audits at $1.5k, done in a spreadsheet. Retain a customs attorney to confirm how metal weight is measured. Build the plugin once patterns repeat.

title: Compute-Heated Pools and Saunas
one_liner: Install small immersion-cooled compute clusters in municipal pools, Ys and recovery studios so the servers pay for the heat.
customer: Municipal pools, YMCAs and hotels with heavy heating bills, recovery studios with saunas, and the AI batch-inference buyers who rent the compute.
problem: Pools and sauna rooms are among the largest energy line items in public and wellness facilities and many public pools are cut when budgets tighten, while AI compute needs cooling and dumps its waste heat.
solution: Deploy a 20-50 kW 'digital boiler' in the plant room that heats pool or sauna water through a heat exchanger, sell the compute to latency-tolerant inference or batch customers, and give the facility free or discounted heat. First product: a single-site pilot funded by a state energy grant and reserved compute.
why_now: A UK pilot at Exmouth Leisure Centre (a 28 kW cluster) reportedly cut the pool's gas use by 62 percent and saved about 24,000 dollars a year while the operator paid for the electricity; AI compute scarcity and edge inference demand are high in 2026 and decarbonization grants are available.
revenue_model: Compute revenue shared with the host, monthly heat fee or discount, and grants; gross margin from selling the heat.
non_obvious_insight: Both sides get paid: the compute buyer gets free cooling and the pool gets free heat, and a pool is a 24/7 constant heat sink unlike offices. The real customer is the compute buyer, with pools as cheap distributed real estate. Capital needs are real, so lead with a grant-funded pilot.
first_30_days: Find a gas-heated pool operator and a champion on the board, sign an MOU, commission a 10-20 kW pilot design with an immersion-cooling vendor, apply to two energy grant programs, and pre-sell reserved compute to two batch-inference customers.

title: Orphan Appliance Parts, Crowdsourced From Repair Techs
one_liner: Quirky (dead 2015) crowdsourced gadgets from hobbyist inventors; the 2026 version prints the discontinued $6 plastic part that keeps a $900 appliance out of the landfill, and pays the repair tech who specced it a royalty.
customer: Independent appliance repair shops (about 10-20 techs per metro market) and multifamily property-maintenance teams that manage hundreds of identical fridges, washers and dishwashers; DIY owners and EU repair cafes come second via marketplace listings.
problem: A brittle plastic piece (fridge door bin, dishwasher rack wheel, washer lid-lock striker, range knob, vacuum gear) is discontinued, backordered for weeks, or OEM-priced at $50-90. Techs condemn a machine over a $6 part, and landlords swap whole units. Techs see the same failure dozens of times but have no channel to monetize that knowledge.
solution: A tech texts a photo and model number. An AI-assisted CAD step plus human check produces a measured model. The part is printed in nylon or carbon-filled PETG through Xometry/Craftcloud-type bureaus, or a small in-house farm. It gets a SKU page, a fit guarantee (free reprint if wrong) and a 10% lifetime royalty to the originating tech. Non-safety-critical parts only: no heating elements, gas, or oven door latches. Shops pay $29/mo for a private request queue, 48-hour dispatch and a discount. Property managers get bulk catalogs per building.
why_now: The EU Right to Repair Directive's national transposition deadline passed on 31 July 2026. It requires spare parts at reasonable prices and bars manufacturers from blocking independent repairers who use compatible or 3D-printed parts. Several US states (CA, NY, MN, OR) have repair laws. Photo-to-CAD tools are good enough and print-on-demand bureaus are cheap. Tariffs have pushed new-appliance prices up, so repair economics are better than in 2015.
revenue_model: Part sales at $18-35 (roughly 50-65% gross margin after print and shipping); $29/mo shop membership; annual bulk contracts with property managers; royalty payouts as the growth loop. Later, license CAD to mid-size OEMs that need cheap R2R-compliant spares for out-of-production models.
non_obvious_insight: Quirky's crowd was the wrong crowd: hobbyist inventors with no ground truth about what breaks. The right crowd already exists in the field: techs who see failure modes daily and lack a way to get paid for that. The right buyer is not the DIYer but a pro or landlord for whom a $12 part avoids a $900 replacement. The orphan-part long tail is what 3D printing is naturally good at, and the R2R text neutralizes OEM opposition.
first_30_days: Pick fridges and dishwashers from 2005-2015. Mine r/appliancerepair, eBay sold listings and out-of-stock parts pages for the 25 most-failed brittle plastics. Model and print them via two bureaus and list on eBay, Etsy and Shopify with the fit guarantee. Recruit 15 local techs from Facebook groups with the royalty offer, and pilot with 3 property managers. Under $10k of spend; target 150 orders.

title: Prize-Money Payout and Tax Rail for Tournaments
one_liner: Payout operations for tournament organizers and esports orgs: one-time player KYC and tax onboarding, treaty-aware withholding, sanctions screening, and multi-currency payment.
customer: Mid-tier tournament organizers (regional leagues, publisher-sanctioned circuits, fighting-game majors) and esports orgs receiving club-program stipends.
problem: Prize money exploded, with $75M at the 2026 Esports World Cup (moved to Paris) and a $20M club partner program across 40 orgs. Payments go to players in dozens of countries, including minors, with tax forms, withholding and sanctions checks, and organizers run it on spreadsheets and wire transfers.
solution: A payout platform with a portable 'player payout profile' (KYC and tax forms collected once), automated withholding by treaty, sanctions screening, escrowed prize pools released on verified results, and payment on local rails. Add visa and travel letter templates and year-end tax reporting.
why_now: Sovereign money inflated prize pools, and the Saudi-Olympic Esports Games partnership ending (2025-10-30) pushes more independent circuits. The compliance burden has grown with the money.
revenue_model: 1-2% of payout volume plus $3-8 per payee, and $500-3,000 per month SaaS for orgs.
non_obvious_insight: Prize pools stopped being a marketing line item and became a payments-and-tax operations problem. The onboarding data is portable across events, so each player carried through one event lowers the cost for the next organizer.
first_30_days: Interview 15 tournament organizers via start.gg and fighting-game communities. Run payouts manually for two events at 1.5% to learn the edge cases, and build the KYC and tax-form intake.

title: Quibi for Home-Care Aides: Serialized Compliance Training
one_liner: Quibi's 90-second premium episodes failed as a consumer subscription; as a serialized vertical drama that home-care aides watch to fulfill their mandatory annual training hours, the same format has a captive, budgeted buyer.
customer: Owners and training directors of home-health and home-care agencies with 20-500 aides. Medicare-certified home health agencies must give each aide annual in-service training (12 hours under federal rules), and many states add annual hours for personal-care aides.
problem: Caregiver turnover benchmarks around 75% in 2025. Required training is slide decks and quizzes that workers click through on phones, yet client falls, infections, abuse-reporting failures and survey citations trace back to it. Agencies pay for training that neither sticks nor improves retention.
solution: A private serialized story of two aides and a difficult client. Each 90-second vertical episode ends on a decision (dementia sundowning, family conflict, suspected neglect); the answer unlocks the next episode. Delivered by SMS or WhatsApp link with no app, in English, Spanish, Tagalog and Haitian Creole. An RN advisor approves content, quiz logs map to training-hour documentation, and supervisors get a completion dashboard. AI-assisted production plus human voice actors keeps a season at low tens of thousands of dollars.
why_now: Microdrama apps are booming: industry trackers put short-drama in-app revenue near $3B in 2025 and forecasts of roughly $8B in 2026, so the habit and format exist. Reported AI-assisted production budgets of $15-80k per series are far below traditional costs. Home-care demand is surging while the workforce shrinks.
revenue_model: $6-10 per aide per month with a $300/mo agency minimum, annual contracts; bespoke episodes on an agency's own policies at $3-5k each; same engine later sold to nursing homes, restaurants and hotels.
non_obvious_insight: Quibi's format was fine and its buyer was wrong. Consumers would not pay $8/mo for premium clips, but mandatory compliance budgets are captive and the outcomes (completion, quiz retention, incident reports, quits) are measurable. Frontline workers already binge microdramas on the same phones, so the drama does the engagement work and the compliance layer does the billing.
first_30_days: Write 6 episodes on three topics (dementia behaviors, fall prevention, abuse reporting) with an RN advisor and produce them for under $5k. Pitch 30 agencies through state home-care association lists and LinkedIn. Run free 30-day pilots at 3 agencies, comparing completion and quiz scores against their current slides, then convert to $500/mo contracts.

title: Medicaid Exemption Evidence Packs for FQHCs
one_liner: An EHR-connected engine that packages state-accepted exemption evidence (medically frail, SUD treatment, disability) so providers keep patients enrolled.
customer: FQHCs, safety-net hospitals and Medicaid MCOs in the 41 expansion states.
problem: Work requirements start Jan 1, 2027 (80 hours a month). Self-attestation is allowed only in 2027 and documentation tightens Jan 1, 2028, with 5.5-6.3M projected coverage losses and a 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hit for hospitals in expansion states. Clinical exemption evidence sits in provider EHRs but nobody packages it for state portals.
solution: Identify likely-exempt patients from problem lists and encounters, generate state-specific attestation and documentation packets, track renewal and verification dates, and give financial counselors a dashboard and patient outreach texts. Wedge is the clinical side, not the state's income-and-hours verification.
why_now: The CMS final rule and state notice deadlines (Aug 31, 2026) are done and system build is underway, so providers have about 3 months of runway. Patient-facing startups exist, but provider-side exemption evidence is mostly open.
revenue_model: $3-8 per covered high-risk member per month, or $75-150 success fee per retained member (an FQHC visit under PPS pays far more than a sliding-fee uninsured visit).
non_obvious_insight: States and their vendors handle income and hours data. The medically-frail and treatment-participation evidence lives with providers, and each retained Medicaid patient is worth many times the fee.
first_30_days: Sign 3 FQHCs in one state through the primary-care association. Manually pull 500 patients' problem lists and produce exemption packets. Measure approval rates, then automate state by state.

title: W-2 Employer-of-Record for AI-Training Experts
one_liner: A task-metered payroll, benefits and contract layer that lets data vendors and labs engage expert contractors as short-term employees without the misclassification and breach exposure of 1099 mass onboarding.
customer: Second-tier human-data vendors (challengers to the Mercor-scale players) and enterprise AI teams running expert-evaluation programs pay an 8-12% margin over payroll.
problem: A class action alleges Surge AI misclassified annotators, Mercor's reported breach exposed about 40k contractors' voice samples, and contractors report declining pay and stress. Enterprise buyers in banking and healthcare won't sign vendors lacking employment and security controls. Standard EOR services can't handle 2-40 hour micro-engagements.
solution: Instant W-2 onboarding across 50 states, with per-task hourly pay, automatic state paid-sick-leave accrual, workers' comp and unemployment tax handled. A data-security wrapper (SSO, ephemeral biometric handling) and portable pay stubs for the worker's income verification round it out.
why_now: Misclassification suits and breach fallout landed in 2025-26, enterprises are now buying expert data and demanding compliance, and a multi-million expert contractor pool has appeared with unprecedented scale.
revenue_model: 8-12% of payroll plus a per-worker admin fee.
non_obvious_insight: Leading marketplaces prefer contractor status because they keep 30-40%, but enterprise and regulated buyers can't absorb the liability. Being the plumbing for challengers, not another marketplace, gives them the enterprise wedge against incumbents.
first_30_days: White-label an existing PEO or EOR to avoid licensing. Sign two small vendors (legal, medical or finance data) for a pilot cohort of 50 W-2 experts. Publish a misclassification-risk checklist to generate inbound.
